_meta.description: Boomerification investable universe — names mapped to the thesis limbs in data/thesis.json. Each record carries the limb it expresses, the age band that pays it, which retiree segment it serves, a thesis note, a conviction score and a froth score.
_meta.conviction_scale: 1 = watching / on the map, 2 = engaged / would own at a price, 3 = core structural position
_meta.froth_scale: 1 = insulated (thesis intact, price not extended), 2 = exposed (narrative priced, needs a pullback), 3 = high froth (crowded, priced for perfection)
_meta.band_scale: Which age band on the cohort clock actually pays this business: pre / gogo / slowgo / nogo / all
_meta.cust_scale: Which retiree the business serves: top = top-decile, median = median under-saved retiree, both

themes_registry.label: Decumulation mechanics
themes_registry.blurb: Businesses whose economics turn on retirees drawing down rather than contributing.

themes_registry.label: Income demand shift
themes_registry.blurb: The composition change in limb A — demand moving from equity beta to guaranteed and contractual cash flow.

themes_registry.label: The wealth transfer
themes_registry.blurb: Direct beneficiaries of assets changing hands, at either the spouse step or the heir step.

themes_registry.label: Advisor break points
themes_registry.blurb: The intermediation share shift that happens when a transfer renegotiates an advice relationship.

themes_registry.label: Labour scarcity
themes_registry.blurb: Owns or supplies scarce licensed labour in a capacity-constrained pipeline.

themes_registry.label: Labour substitution
themes_registry.blurb: Sells the capital that replaces the labour limb C says is disappearing.

themes_registry.label: Services inflation
themes_registry.blurb: Pricing power derived from non-tradable service wage inflation.

themes_registry.label: Go-go fade
themes_registry.blurb: Demand is paid by the 65-74 band, whose population peaks around 2030 and then declines.

themes_registry.label: Slow-go rotation
themes_registry.blurb: Demand is paid by the 75-84 band — the fastest-growing band through 2035.

themes_registry.label: Care volumes
themes_registry.blurb: Volume leverage to care hours and admissions rather than to reimbursement rate.

themes_registry.label: Aging in place
themes_registry.blurb: The revealed preference to stay home — modification, mobility, in-home services.

themes_registry.label: Silver inventory
themes_registry.blurb: Release of the owner-occupied housing stock as the cohort ages through care transitions.

themes_registry.label: Reimbursement risk
themes_registry.blurb: Flag, not a thesis. Earnings depend on a government-set rate that limb E says is politically exposed.

themes_registry.label: Medicare Advantage
themes_registry.blurb: Enrolment growth from the cohort clock, against a rate environment set annually by CMS.

themes_registry.label: Longevity medtech
themes_registry.blurb: Devices whose procedure volume scales directly with the 75+ population.

themes_registry.label: Sensory decline
themes_registry.blurb: Hearing, vision and dental — the most predictable, least reimbursement-exposed age curves in medtech.

themes_registry.label: Cognitive decline
themes_registry.blurb: Dementia diagnosis, treatment and memory care — the largest unmet cost in the no-go band.

themes_registry.label: End of life
themes_registry.blurb: Hospice, death care and the estate settlement chain.

themes_registry.label: Japan template
themes_registry.blurb: Operates in the market that ran this demographic experiment thirty years early.

themes_registry.label: Immigration swing
themes_registry.blurb: P&L is directly sensitive to the immigration policy that is limb C's main falsifier.

themes_registry.label: Entitlement cliff
themes_registry.blurb: Exposed to the trust-fund and benefit-formula step functions in limb E.

themes_registry.label: Active adult
themes_registry.blurb: Purpose-built 55+ housing — the go-go band's housing decision.

themes_registry.label: GLP-1 / morbidity compression
themes_registry.blurb: Flag. The live version of limb D's falsifier — a healthier elderly population pushes the care curve right.

themes_registry.label: Median retiree
themes_registry.blurb: Serves the under-saved majority rather than the top decile — different demand curve, different policy exposure.

themes_registry.label: Top-decile retiree
themes_registry.blurb: Serves the wealth-holding decile that does not decumulate — discretionary, legacy and estate spending.

themes_registry.label: No-go band demand
themes_registry.blurb: Paid by the 85+ band specifically — the fastest-compounding population on the clock and the most care-intensive.

private_companies.note: Second-largest US retirement recordkeeper. Owned by Great-West Lifeco (GWO.TO) — the listed route in.
The largest private counterweight in both limb A and limb B. Unlistable, but its share moves are the best read on whether the intermediation shift in limb B is real.
Client-owned. Its advice business is the price anchor the whole limb B fee-compression argument runs into.
Partnership. Its client book is the oldest in the industry — the cleanest natural experiment in transfer-driven advisor attrition.
The large private RIA aggregators. Their M&A multiples are the mark for the listed comps in the wt vertical.

private_companies.n: Addepar / Orion / Vanilla / Wealth.com / Trust & Will
private_companies.note: Wealth and estate technology, all private. The estate-planning software layer is the least-penetrated part of limb B.
Taken private in 2024. Removed a listed pure-play from the advisor-platform trade and left SEIC and MORN as the closest reads.

private_companies.n: Atria Senior Living / Sunrise Senior Living
private_companies.note: Large private senior housing operators. Their occupancy and labour-cost commentary is the sector read-through for BKD, WELL and VTR.
Mobility and stairlift manufacturers — the aging-in-place hardware layer is almost entirely private, which is why the listed expression runs through HD, LOW and IBP instead.
Venture-funded in-home care and senior-focused payors. Watch as competitive threats to ADUS and ALHC rather than as investments.

_meta.private_note: Large parts of this thesis — estate technology, mobility hardware, private RIAs, senior housing operators — are structurally private. Where the best expression is unlistable, the record says so rather than substituting a worse listed proxy.
_meta.coverage_note: v1 universe. Deliberately excludes the raw-materials and AI/semiconductor chains covered by the sibling hard-assets-research and ai-hardware-research maps. Corporate actions are checked automatically each run by scripts/fetch_fundamentals.py against SEC EDGAR; renames and delistings surface as flags rather than as silently wrong tickers.

companies.name: Equitable Holdings
companies.thesis_note: The cleanest listed expression of limb A's composition shift. Equitable writes registered index-linked annuities — the product category built precisely for a household that wants equity participation with a floor, which is what the pre-retirement and early-retirement bands actually demand. It also owns a majority of AllianceBernstein, so the asset-management fee stream sits alongside the spread business. The reason this is core rather than merely interesting: RILA demand is a direct read on the behavioural shift the thesis predicts, and it is growing from a small base against a very large addressable pool of 55-64 households. What would break it: a rate collapse that destroys the spread economics, or a regulatory move on index-linked product disclosure.

companies.name: Corebridge Financial
companies.thesis_note: The AIG retirement spinout, and the closest thing to a pure listed bet on Americans converting savings into contractual income. Fixed and index annuity sales plus a very large in-force block, sold at a persistent discount to book that reflects the market's structural discomfort with spread businesses rather than anything specific to this one. The limb A argument is that the flow into guaranteed income is not cyclical — it is the cohort clock expressing itself through a product choice. Risk: it is a rate-and-credit levered balance sheet, and a credit cycle hits it before the demographics rescue it.

companies.name: Jackson Financial
companies.thesis_note: Variable annuity specialist with an unusually aggressive capital return programme funded by the run-off of a large legacy block. The bull case is that the market treats the hedging complexity as a permanent discount when the underlying flow — retirees buying downside protection — is exactly what limb A predicts grows. The bear case is genuine: the hedge programme is opaque from outside, and a disorderly equity drawdown tests it in a way the disclosure does not let you pre-verify.

companies.name: Voya Financial
companies.thesis_note: Sits at the exact chokepoint limb A cares about: the workplace plan, where the rollover decision gets made. Recordkeeping is a low-margin business whose value is the option on capturing assets at the retirement transition rather than losing them to an IRA provider. The thesis question is whether Voya converts that adjacency; the honest answer is that the industry's historical conversion rate is poor and Fidelity takes most of the prize.

companies.name: Principal Financial Group
companies.thesis_note: Small-and-mid-business retirement plans plus asset management and a growing guaranteed-income shelf. The SMB plan franchise is a genuinely defensible niche — the segment is too fragmented for the mega-recordkeepers to serve efficiently — and it is where the median retiree in the thesis actually holds their savings. Slower-moving than EQH or CRBG on the product shift, but the distribution is stickier.

companies.name: Apollo Global Management
companies.thesis_note: The structural winner of limb A if the limb is right. Athene originates retirement liabilities — annuities sold to the cohort — and Apollo invests them in privately originated credit at a spread. That is not a levered bet on markets; it is a manufacturing business whose raw material is exactly the demand the thesis says grows. It is also the sharpest illustration of why limb A is a composition trade rather than a supply shock: retiree money does not leave the system, it changes wrapper, and the wrapper owner captures the spread. Risk concentrates in credit quality at the point in the cycle when origination volume looks best — and the regulatory scrutiny of insurer-affiliated private credit is rising, not falling.
companies.froth_note: Narrative fully discovered; the private-credit-plus-insurance model is now the consensus structure. Own it for the flywheel, but expect no multiple support in a credit wobble.

companies.name: KKR & Co
companies.thesis_note: Same flywheel as Apollo — Global Atlantic supplies the retirement liabilities, the private markets platform invests them — but the insurance leg is a smaller share of the whole, so it is a diluted version of the limb A trade attached to a stronger diversified franchise. Own for the combination rather than for the demographic purity.

companies.name: Ares Management
companies.thesis_note: Private credit is the supply side of the income demand limb A describes, and Ares is the highest-quality pure expression of it. The demographic argument is straightforward: a cohort that needs contractual cash flow and a wealth channel newly able to access private credit through evergreen vehicles meet in the middle. The risk is equally straightforward — this is a spread business selling illiquidity to a client base that has never tested the liquidity terms in a real drawdown.

companies.name: Blackstone
companies.thesis_note: The most advanced distributor of private assets into the individual wealth channel, which is where limbs A and B intersect: transferred and decumulating wealth being re-intermediated into products with higher fees and longer lockups. BREIT taught the whole industry what happens when semi-liquid vehicles meet a redemption wave, and that lesson is the main risk to the entire evergreen distribution thesis.

companies.name: Blue Owl Capital
companies.thesis_note: Built deliberately around permanent and perpetual capital and heavily weighted to the wealth channel — structurally the right shape for limb A, since the liability side does not run. The concentration in a narrow slice of direct lending is the offsetting concern; permanent capital protects the manager, not the underlying credit.

companies.name: Reinsurance Group of America
companies.thesis_note: The purest listed way to take the other side of longevity risk professionally. RGA reinsures both mortality and longevity, which means it is one of very few businesses whose core competence is pricing exactly the variable this thesis is built on. Pension risk transfer — corporates offloading longevity exposure — is a structurally growing flow driven by the same clock. The tail risk is symmetrical and real: an unexpected extension of life expectancy is a loss event on the longevity book, and morbidity compression under GLP-1s is not a hypothetical version of that.

companies.name: BlackRock
companies.thesis_note: Owns the target-date default that most of the cohort's workplace savings sit in, and has been pushing hardest on embedding guaranteed income inside the default option. If in-plan annuitisation becomes standard, BlackRock captures the transition rather than losing assets at the rollover. That is a genuine limb A option — but it is one option inside a very large company, so the demographic exposure per dollar invested is thin.

companies.name: T. Rowe Price
companies.thesis_note: Included as the counter-example rather than the position. T. Rowe is the clearest listed illustration of limb A's negative case: a business whose economics depend on continuous contributions into active products from an accumulating cohort that is shrinking, while the decumulating cohort withdraws. Strong target-date franchise and a genuine income push, but the structural flow direction is against it. Watch it as the control variable for whether the flow reversal is showing up at all.

companies.name: CNO Financial Group
companies.thesis_note: Sells life, supplemental health and annuity products to middle-income Americans aged 55 and over — precisely the median retiree the thesis says gets ignored when people describe 'the wealthy boomer'. That segment is far larger by headcount than the top decile, has real coverage gaps that Medicare does not fill, and is served by almost nobody with scale. The legacy long-term-care block is the standing risk and the reason the stock trades where it does.

companies.name: Unum Group
companies.thesis_note: On the map as a risk study rather than a long. Unum carries a large legacy long-term-care block written decades ago on assumptions about longevity and care cost that the thesis says were wrong in the direction that hurts. It is the cleanest listed demonstration that aging is not universally a revenue event — for some balance sheets it is the liability. Watch the reserve reviews as an independent read on care-cost inflation.

companies.name: Great-West Lifeco
companies.thesis_note: The listed route into Empower, the second-largest US retirement recordkeeper and therefore one of the two businesses best positioned to see the rollover decision before anyone else. Buried inside a Canadian insurance conglomerate, so the exposure is diluted and the disclosure is thin. Held as the read-through rather than the position.

companies.name: Morgan Stanley
companies.thesis_note: The largest listed beneficiary of limb B, and the one where the transfer mechanics are most explicit in the business model. Morgan Stanley's wealth franchise spans self-directed, advisor-led and workplace equity plans, which means it can meet the heir at whichever channel they arrive through rather than losing them at the break point. The workplace stock-plan business is the genuinely differentiated asset here: it acquires the next-generation client while they are still accumulating, years before the inheritance lands. What would break it: fee compression arriving faster than net new assets, or the demonstration that heirs consolidate away from full-service regardless of channel breadth.
companies.froth_note: Wealth-management multiple re-rating is well advanced. The demographic story is understood; the entry question is price, not thesis.

companies.name: LPL Financial Holdings
companies.thesis_note: The purest listed expression of the intermediation share shift. LPL does not compete for the end client — it supplies the platform, custody, compliance and technology to independent advisors who do, and it grows by recruiting advisors away from wirehouses and banks. Limb B says every transfer event is a moment when both the client relationship and the advisor's own affiliation get renegotiated; LPL is levered to both sides of that. Advisor demographics add a second engine: the average advisor is old enough that succession is itself a recruiting event. Risk is that the model's economics are meaningfully rate-sensitive through client cash sweep, which is a real earnings driver dressed as a rounding item.
companies.froth_note: Recruiting momentum is priced. The cash-sweep sensitivity means a rate-cut cycle hits earnings while the demographic story is unchanged — that gap is the entry.

companies.name: Raymond James Financial
companies.thesis_note: Culturally the most advisor-friendly of the large full-service firms, which matters more than it sounds: in limb B, the firm that retains advisors retains the client books that carry the transfer. Multi-affiliation options let it hold an advisor who wants independence rather than lose them to LPL. Cash sweep economics and a bank balance sheet make the earnings noisier than the franchise quality suggests.

companies.name: Charles Schwab
companies.thesis_note: Custodian to a very large share of the independent RIA channel — the channel limb B says takes share at each transfer break point. Schwab wins whether the assets sit with the advisor or the self-directed heir, which is an unusually good structural position. The offsetting reality is that the earnings model is a bank: net interest revenue on client cash dominates, and that has nothing to do with demographics.

companies.name: Ameriprise Financial
companies.thesis_note: The hybrid: an advice franchise sitting on top of both an asset manager and an annuity writer, which means it monetises limb A and limb B in the same client relationship. Strong execution and disciplined capital return. The concern is client-book age — Ameriprise's advisor base has historically served an older client, which is the transfer exposure cutting the wrong way if retention at the heir step is poor.

companies.name: Stifel Financial
companies.thesis_note: Persistent advisor recruiter in the mid-market, with the same transfer-driven recruiting tailwind as LPL and RJF but a smaller platform and a capital-markets business that adds cyclicality unrelated to the thesis. On the map as the smaller-cap version of the trade.

companies.name: Northern Trust
companies.thesis_note: The most direct listed exposure to the actual mechanics of the transfer: trust administration, estate settlement and multigenerational family office services for exactly the top-decile households that hold the assets and will not decumulate. This is limb B's execution layer — the work that happens when an estate settles, not the marketing around it. Structurally advantaged, chronically operationally inefficient, and the earnings are rate-driven in the short run regardless.

companies.name: BNY (Bank of New York Mellon)
companies.thesis_note: Pershing is the second major RIA and broker-dealer custody platform, which gives BNY the same structural position as Schwab in limb B — but it is a small part of a very large custody and markets-infrastructure business. Diluted exposure, held for the read-through on advisor-channel flows. TICKER CORRECTED 2026-08-07: the company rebranded and now trades as BNY; the universe carried the stale BK symbol, which is why the market robot could not price it.

companies.name: SEI Investments
companies.thesis_note: Sells the operating system to advisors, banks and trust companies — the unglamorous back-office layer that has to be repapered every time an advice relationship moves. With Envestnet taken private, SEI is one of the few remaining listed ways to own the advisor-technology layer directly rather than through a wirehouse. Growth has been pedestrian for years; the thesis is that the transfer wave forces a technology refresh cycle it has not yet had.

companies.name: Morningstar
companies.thesis_note: Data and workstation software sold to the advisor channel, plus a managed-portfolio business that scales with fee-based conversion. Benefits from the same structural move to fee-based advice that limb B describes. Priced as a quality compounder, which leaves little room for the thesis to add anything.

companies.name: Intuit
companies.thesis_note: Tax complexity rises sharply at two points the thesis cares about: the retirement transition, where withdrawal sequencing and Roth conversion decisions arrive at once, and estate settlement. Intuit owns the consumer end of that. But the demographic contribution to a business this size is a rounding error, and the multiple prices AI-driven expansion rather than anything in this thesis.
companies.froth_note: Priced on AI attach and pricing power, not on any demographic argument. Included for map completeness only.

companies.name: Thomson Reuters
companies.thesis_note: Supplies the tax, trust and estate professionals who actually execute transfers. Recurring, entrenched, and levered to the volume of estate work rather than to asset prices — a genuinely differentiated way to hold limb B. Priced accordingly, and the demographic share of the story is small.

companies.name: UBS Group
companies.thesis_note: The largest non-US private wealth franchise, which matters because the transfer is not a purely American phenomenon — Europe and Asia run the same clock on a different lag. Still digesting the Credit Suisse integration, which dominates the near-term equity story and drowns out any demographic signal.

companies.name: Interactive Brokers
companies.thesis_note: The destination when the heir decides they do not want an advisor at all. That is a real and underdiscussed branch of limb B — the transfer does not only move the relationship between intermediaries, it sometimes removes the intermediary. IBKR is the cheapest operator in the industry, which is what wins that customer.

companies.name: AMN Healthcare Services
companies.thesis_note: The listed proxy for the clinical labour shortage limb C describes. Travel nursing collapsed from its pandemic peak and the equity was destroyed with it, which is the setup: the cyclical bill-rate normalisation is over-extrapolated while the structural nursing pipeline problem is unchanged and the 85+ population that consumes nursing hours is about to double. The honest risk is that hospitals have permanently insourced their float pools, which would make the structural argument true and the equity still wrong. CORRECTION 2026-08-07: the iteration-2 raise was wrong and is reversed, harder than it was made. Revenue fell from a $5.24bn peak (CY2022) to $2.73bn (CY2025) and operating margin went from +12.3% to NEGATIVE, a swing of -10.0pp. The structural nursing shortage is real — ECI and AACN both confirm it — but it did not accrue to the staffing intermediary. Bill-rate normalisation destroyed the spread. 'Whoever supplies the scarce labour has pricing power' is false for agencies; the pricing power sat with the operators who employ directly. Cut to 1.

companies.name: Cross Country Healthcare
companies.thesis_note: The smaller, higher-beta version of the AMN trade with the same structural argument and less balance-sheet room to survive a long normalisation. On the map for optionality rather than as a position.

companies.name: EMCOR Group
companies.thesis_note: The best-run owner of scarce skilled trade labour in the listed market, and the clearest demonstration of limb C's economics. EMCOR's competitive advantage is not technology or scale in the usual sense — it is that it employs electricians, pipefitters and sheet-metal workers who cannot be hired quickly at any price, in a market where the retiring cohort of licensed tradespeople is not being replaced. That converts a fragmented contracting business into a capacity-constrained one with genuine pricing power and rising margins. The demographic bull case and the datacentre-construction bull case happen to point the same way right now, which is exactly why the froth score is 3: you are not being paid to take the demographic risk at this price.
companies.froth_note: Has re-rated hard on the AI-datacentre construction narrative. The labour-scarcity thesis is intact and durable; the entry price assumes a construction cycle that does not roll over. Wait for the cycle to scare people.

companies.name: Comfort Systems USA
companies.thesis_note: Same structural argument as EMCOR — the scarce asset is the licensed mechanical workforce, not the equipment — with more concentrated exposure to industrial and datacentre construction. Superb operator. The valuation now embeds a multi-year capex boom, so the demographic labour thesis is being given away free on top of a cyclical bet you may not want.
companies.froth_note: Among the most extended names in the universe on any historical measure. Structural thesis unimpaired; price offers no margin for the cycle.

companies.name: MYR Group
companies.thesis_note: Linework is the sharpest single example of limb C: journeyman linemen require years of apprenticeship, the incumbent workforce is old, the work cannot be offshored or automated, and grid investment demand is rising regardless. MYR is a smaller, more volatile way to own that labour pool than Quanta, with more project-execution risk and correspondingly cheaper.

companies.name: Quanta Services
companies.thesis_note: The largest skilled-labour pool in North American utility infrastructure and the only contractor operating its own linework training academies at scale — which is the correct strategic response to limb C and a real moat. Also the single most crowded expression of the grid-investment theme, so the demographic argument arrives already paid for.
companies.froth_note: Grid capex narrative fully priced. Own the labour scarcity thesis here only on a cycle scare.

companies.name: IES Holdings
companies.thesis_note: Small-cap electrical contractor that has compounded exceptionally through the same labour-scarcity dynamic. The thesis works; the share price has already reflected several years of it, and liquidity is thin enough that an exit in a drawdown is not free.

companies.name: APi Group
companies.thesis_note: The most attractive shape in the labour vertical: statutorily mandated fire and life-safety inspection generates recurring, non-discretionary, price-escalating revenue performed by licensed technicians who are in the same shortage as every other trade. Mandated demand plus scarce labour is the combination limb C is looking for, and unlike the construction contractors it does not need a capex cycle to work.

companies.name: Limbach Holdings
companies.thesis_note: Deliberately shifting mix from construction bids to owner-direct maintenance, which converts the scarce-labour asset into recurring revenue at better margins. Small, illiquid, and executing well on a strategy that is correct for limb C.

companies.name: Covista (formerly Adtalem Global Education)
companies.thesis_note: Owns Chamberlain University, the largest US nursing school, plus Walden and the medical and veterinary schools. This is the cleanest way to own limb C's binding constraint rather than its symptom: the nursing shortage is not a demand problem, it is a training-capacity problem — schools turn away qualified applicants for lack of faculty and clinical placements. Whoever owns accredited capacity in a capacity-constrained pipeline has pricing power that is independent of the economic cycle, and the demand behind it is the 85+ population arithmetic. Risk is entirely regulatory: for-profit education lives at the mercy of Title IV rulemaking, and that risk is genuinely bimodal. TICKER CORRECTED 2026-08-07: renamed from Adtalem to Covista and now trades as CVSA (10-K filed 2026-08-06; SEC former-name chain DeVry -> Adtalem -> Covista). The universe carried ATGE. Filings support the position: revenue +9.9% CAGR CY2019-CY2025 with operating margin +3.7pp — the only one of the three care-labour names raised in iteration 2 that the numbers actually back.
companies.froth_note: Has re-rated substantially as the market recognised the nursing-capacity story. Still the right structural asset; size for the regulatory tail.

companies.name: Grand Canyon Education
companies.thesis_note: Services provider to Grand Canyon University with a growing weight in healthcare and nursing programmes, including hybrid clinical sites that address exactly the placement bottleneck constraining the pipeline. Cleaner regulatory posture than the traditional for-profits and consistently well operated.

companies.name: Lincoln Educational Services
companies.thesis_note: Trains the HVAC technicians, welders, electricians and automotive technicians whose retirement is limb C's core claim. Enrolment growth is being pulled by employer demand rather than pushed by marketing, which is the healthy version of this business model. Small-cap, regulatory-exposed, and the most direct listed play on the trades pipeline specifically.

companies.name: Universal Technical Institute
companies.thesis_note: Transport, energy and skilled-trades technician training, now diversified into healthcare programmes through the Concorde acquisition — which puts it in both halves of limb C's shortage at once. Manufacturer-sponsored programmes give it a demand signal most education businesses lack.

companies.name: Korn Ferry
companies.thesis_note: An under-considered angle on limb C: the retirement wave is happening in the C-suite and the board as much as on the shop floor, and succession planning is a paid service. Cyclical like all search businesses, which obscures the structural driver, but the consulting and assessment mix makes it less purely cyclical than it was.

companies.name: Healthcare Services Group
companies.chain_layer: Outsourced dining & housekeeping to care facilities
companies.thesis_note: Outsourced support labour to skilled nursing and senior living — sits at the exact intersection of limbs C and D, and demonstrates the collision between them. Volume grows with the care population; margin is squeezed by the same wage inflation that creates the volume. A structurally difficult business that is nonetheless an excellent monitoring instrument for whether care-labour costs are accelerating.

companies.name: Rockwell Automation
companies.thesis_note: The most US-weighted large industrial automation franchise, which matters because limb C's labour scarcity is a US phenomenon before it is a global one. The investment case is that manufacturers facing a shrinking pool of experienced operators and technicians substitute capital for labour, and that this substitution is structural rather than cyclical. The counter-evidence is that Rockwell's orders have been thoroughly cyclical whenever tested.

companies.name: Emerson Electric
companies.thesis_note: Process automation for industries losing their most experienced operators — the knowledge-capture argument is real: as veteran process engineers retire, the control system has to encode judgment that used to live in people's heads. Well-positioned, well-run, and largely priced as an industrial compounder rather than a demographic beneficiary.

companies.name: Symbotic
companies.thesis_note: Direct labour substitution in the warehouse — the clearest one-for-one replacement of scarce hourly labour in the universe. Customer concentration is extreme and the accounting has required restatement, which together mean the thesis quality and the security quality are very different things here.
companies.froth_note: Priced as a high-growth technology asset. Any thesis contribution is swamped by execution and concentration risk.

companies.name: Keyence
companies.thesis_note: The highest-margin business in industrial automation, selling the sensing layer that makes labour substitution possible. Also a Japan-template holding: Keyence grew into a domestic market that ran this exact demographic experiment thirty years early, which is the strongest available evidence that capital substitution follows labour scarcity rather than merely coinciding with it.

companies.name: Fanuc
companies.thesis_note: The incumbent in factory robotics, with the Japan-template argument attached: Japanese manufacturers automated in direct response to a shrinking working-age population, and Fanuc was the supplier. Chinese domestic competition has compressed the industry's pricing power materially, which is the main reason this is not a higher conviction position.

companies.name: Intuitive Surgical
companies.thesis_note: Sits in both limbs at once: procedure volumes scale with the aging population (limb D) while the system extends the productive output of a scarce surgeon workforce (limb C). That dual exposure is genuinely rare in this universe. It is also among the most expensive assets in healthcare on any measure, so the demographic tailwind is fully capitalised.
companies.froth_note: Quality is not in question; price is. Nothing in this thesis is un-priced here.

companies.name: Zebra Technologies
companies.thesis_note: Scanning, mobile computing and workflow software that raises output per frontline worker — the incremental rather than wholesale version of labour substitution, and therefore the version that actually gets bought in a shortage. Cyclical demand tied to retail and logistics capex.

companies.name: The Ensign Group
companies.thesis_note: The best operator in the least-loved corner of the care universe, and the sharpest test of whether limb D can be owned profitably despite limb C. Ensign's model is decentralised acquisition of underperforming skilled nursing facilities and improvement of local operations — which is precisely a labour-management competence, in an industry where labour is the binding constraint and the cost problem. That is why it deserves the premium the market gives it. The demand side is arithmetic: skilled nursing census is driven by the 85+ population, which roughly doubles by 2040. The risk is unambiguous and concentrated: Medicaid is the dominant payor, Medicaid is a state budget line, and state budgets are limb E's problem arriving locally. REPRICED 2026-08-07: CMS data shows SNF days per 1,000 beneficiaries fell 31% over 2014-2024, so the end market grows at roughly population minus 3.6% a year rather than with the population. The operating argument is untouched and the age gradient is steeper than assumed (7.0x at 85+ versus 65-74) — but conviction moves from 3 to 2 because the magnitude of the tailwind was overstated, not because the business got worse. CORRECTION 2026-08-07: the iteration-1 downgrade to 2 was wrong and is reversed. SEC filings show revenue compounding 16.4% a year CY2019-CY2025 and operating margin UP 2.1pp — achieved straight through the decade when per-capita SNF days fell 31%. The utilisation finding is a market-SIZE warning, not a company-revenue prediction: in a sector this fragmented a disciplined consolidator can outgrow a shrinking per-capita market for a long time, and this one demonstrably did. Back to 3.
companies.froth_note: Compounder multiple in a sector priced for distress — the gap is earned but leaves nothing for a reimbursement shock.

companies.name: Addus HomeCare
companies.thesis_note: Personal care services delivered in the home — the single largest and least glamorous category of aging-in-place demand, and the one the cohort actually chooses. The structural case is strong on both sides: demand is the 85+ arithmetic plus the revealed preference to stay home, and supply is constrained because the caregiver workforce is difficult to recruit at Medicaid reimbursement rates. Addus has consolidated a fragmented market competently. The two risks are the same two facts stated as threats: reimbursement is largely Medicaid, and caregiver wage inflation is limb C landing directly on the cost line. Immigration policy hits this P&L more directly than almost anything else in the universe.

companies.name: Aveanna Healthcare
companies.thesis_note: Home-based care with a large paediatric private-duty nursing business alongside the adult home health segment, so it is only partly a thesis holding. Heavily levered balance sheet — this is a rate-and-reimbursement equity before it is a demographic one.

companies.name: BrightSpring Health Services
companies.thesis_note: Combines home and community-based care with a large pharmacy business serving long-term-care and behavioural populations. The pharmacy leg is the interesting part for this thesis: dispensing to institutionalised and home-bound seniors is a volume business that scales with the no-go band and is less exposed to the care-labour cost spiral than the services leg. Complex story, complex capital structure.

companies.name: Chemed
companies.thesis_note: An odd conglomerate — the largest US hospice operator bolted to a plumbing franchise — but the hospice business is one of the purest demographic annuities available. Hospice admissions are driven by deaths, and the death rate in the cohort is the most forecastable number in the entire thesis. Medicare per-diem reimbursement makes it a limb E exposure too; the plumbing business is uncorrelated ballast that arguably has no business being there. REPRICED 2026-08-07: hospice was the only care category where per-capita utilisation ROSE over 2014-2024, +21% in days per 1,000, while SNF fell 31% and home health fell 32%. Terminal demand cannot be moved to a cheaper site of care, deferred by better health management, or managed down by a payment model. Conviction 2 to 3.

companies.name: Encompass Health
companies.thesis_note: The largest inpatient rehabilitation operator. Demand is driven by stroke, hip fracture and joint replacement recovery — three conditions whose incidence tracks the 75+ population almost mechanically. Consistent bed expansion into a demand curve that arrives on schedule, which is exactly the shape limb D wants. Medicare-dominated payor mix is the standing limb E exposure.

companies.name: U.S. Physical Therapy
companies.thesis_note: Outpatient physical therapy is the post-acute step for the joint replacements and fall injuries that scale with the slow-go band, and it is delivered by licensed therapists who are themselves in shortage — limb C and limb D in one P&L again. Clinic-level partnership economics have been durable. Reimbursement per visit has been ground down for years, which is the structural headwind against the volume tailwind.

companies.name: Option Care Health
companies.thesis_note: Home infusion is a genuine site-of-care shift story with the aging tailwind underneath it: therapies that used to require a hospital chair are delivered at home, cheaper, to a population that is growing and prefers to be at home. National scale in a business where scale genuinely matters for payor contracting. Watch drug-mix economics — the margin is a spread on the drug, which makes it vulnerable to changes in a single large therapy.

companies.name: DaVita
companies.thesis_note: End-stage renal disease incidence rises with age and with diabetes prevalence, both of which the cohort supplies. Duopoly economics and heavy buybacks. Two live threats sit against it: GLP-1 drugs plausibly reduce the diabetic progression that feeds the patient pool, and the commercial-versus-government payor mix is the entire margin. A structurally exposed business rather than a structurally advantaged one.

companies.name: RadNet
companies.thesis_note: Imaging volume scales with age almost linearly, and outpatient imaging keeps taking share from hospital settings on cost. The additional angle that matters for limb C: radiologists are in acute shortage, and RadNet's AI reading tools are a direct productivity response to that — labour substitution inside a care business. Capital intensive, and the equity has already priced a good deal of the AI narrative.

companies.name: Labcorp
companies.thesis_note: Test volume per capita rises steadily with age, so the demographic tailwind is real but slow and thoroughly understood. Hospital outreach acquisitions are the growth engine rather than demography. Held as a low-volatility way to be long care volumes with no thesis edge in it.

companies.name: Privia Health
companies.thesis_note: Asset-light physician enablement — Privia provides the technology, contracting and administrative layer to independent practices rather than employing the doctors or owning the buildings. Given that limb C predicts clinical labour cost inflation and limb E predicts reimbursement pressure, the asset-light model is the structurally correct shape: it participates in care volume growth without owning the two lines most likely to be squeezed. Growth depends on practice recruitment, which is a real execution constraint.

companies.name: Astrana Health
companies.thesis_note: Manages risk-bearing physician networks serving heavily Medicare Advantage and Medicaid populations. The value-based model is the correct long-term answer to limb E's cost pressure, but the sector's history — Cano, Bright, and the wider retreat from senior primary care — is a warning that taking medical risk on an elderly population is genuinely hard, not merely unfashionable.

companies.name: The Pennant Group
companies.thesis_note: The Ensign spinout, running the same decentralised local-leadership operating model across home health, hospice and a small senior living portfolio. Inherits a genuinely differentiated culture in an industry where operating competence is the whole game. Small, illiquid, and has re-rated a long way on execution.

companies.name: National HealthCare Corporation
companies.thesis_note: Conservatively financed, family-influenced skilled nursing and senior living operator with a long record and an unusually clean balance sheet for the sector. Slow, unfashionable, and precisely the kind of asset that survives the reimbursement scenarios that kill levered competitors.

companies.name: UnitedHealth Group
companies.thesis_note: The largest Medicare Advantage franchise attached to the largest care-delivery and pharmacy-services business. Enrolment growth is pure cohort clock. The last two years demonstrated the limb E thesis in real time and at painful cost: medical cost trend accelerated, risk-model and rate changes bit, and the political exposure of the MA programme became explicit rather than theoretical. That is the whole limb E argument as a case study — the demographics deliver the members, the government sets the price.

companies.name: Humana
companies.thesis_note: The purest listed Medicare Advantage exposure, which makes it the purest expression of limb E's central tension: enrolment is guaranteed by demography, profitability is set annually by CMS and by a medical cost trend driven partly by limb C's wage inflation. If you want to hold the view that MA rates normalise favourably, this is the highest-beta way to do it — and if you want a live instrument for tracking limb E's political risk, this is also it.

companies.name: Alignment Healthcare
companies.thesis_note: Smaller MA insurer built around its own clinical-management technology, gaining share while the incumbents retrench. The bull case is that a purpose-built senior-care insurer manages cost trend better than a general insurer bolting on a segment. Unproven through a full rate cycle, and the sector's failures outnumber its successes.

companies.name: Elevance Health
companies.thesis_note: Diversified across commercial, Medicaid and Medicare, which dilutes the demographic exposure but also dilutes the single-programme political risk. Medicaid exposure is its own limb E problem — state budgets are where the entitlement squeeze shows up first and most brutally.

companies.name: Evolent Health
companies.thesis_note: Sells specialty care cost management — oncology, cardiology, musculoskeletal — to payors under performance-based contracts. This is the correct structural answer to limb E: if the political pressure lands on healthcare pricing, the businesses that reduce cost get bought rather than cut. Execution has been inconsistent and the contract economics transfer real risk onto Evolent's own P&L.

companies.name: Edwards Lifesciences
companies.thesis_note: The purest age trade in medical devices. Aortic stenosis is a disease of the old — prevalence rises steeply after 75 — and transcatheter aortic valve replacement converts what used to be inoperable or open-heart surgery into a procedure an eighty-five-year-old can survive. That combination means the addressable population and the treatable share of it both grow with the cohort clock, and the expansion into asymptomatic patients enlarges the pool again. Volume-driven rather than price-driven, which is exactly the shape limb D wants given limb E's reimbursement risk. Competitive risk from Abbott and Medtronic in the newer structural-heart categories is the main thing to watch, not demand.
companies.froth_note: Well understood as a demographic asset; the multiple reflects it. Entry has historically come from quarterly volume wobbles rather than from thesis damage.

companies.name: Stryker
companies.thesis_note: Hip and knee replacement volumes track the 65-84 population directly, and Stryker has taken share consistently through the Mako robotic platform — which also carries a limb C angle, extending scarce surgeon capacity. Best-in-class operator with a diversified base that reduces the pure demographic leverage. Priced as quality.

companies.name: Zimmer Biomet
companies.thesis_note: The most levered large-cap to joint replacement volume specifically, and the cheapest way to own that volume. The persistent discount reflects a genuine problem — pricing per implant erodes annually while volume grows — so the thesis holds only if volume growth outruns price erosion. The demographic arithmetic says it should; a decade of share loss says execution has not.

companies.name: Globus Medical
companies.thesis_note: Degenerative spine disease is an age curve, and the NuVasive merger created genuine scale in a consolidating market. Robotics and navigation attach carries the same surgeon-productivity argument as Stryker's Mako. Integration risk is the near-term variable.

companies.name: Smith+Nephew
companies.thesis_note: Perennial self-help story in orthopaedics, but the advanced wound care franchise is the underappreciated demographic asset: chronic wounds — diabetic foot ulcers, pressure injuries, venous ulcers — are overwhelmingly a condition of the old and the immobile, and the 85+ population is the input. Cheap for structural reasons that have persisted through several management teams.

companies.name: Alcon
companies.thesis_note: Cataract is the most universal age-driven procedure in medicine — effectively everyone who lives long enough develops one, and the surgery is high-volume, low-risk and increasingly elective in its timing. Alcon leads intraocular lenses, and the mix shift toward premium presbyopia-correcting lenses is the crucial economic point: those are patient-paid, out of pocket, above the reimbursed base. That combination of biologically inevitable volume and a private-pay premium layer is the rarest thing in this universe — an age-driven medtech franchise that is structurally insulated from limb E. Watch premium lens penetration as the single most important operating metric.

companies.name: Bausch + Lomb
companies.chain_layer: Eye health — surgical, vision care, pharma
companies.thesis_note: The same eye-health demographics as Alcon in a much messier package: the Bausch Health parent relationship, the associated leverage and the overhang from that structure dominate the equity. The underlying assets are exposed to the right curve; the wrapper is the problem.

companies.name: Sonova Holding
companies.thesis_note: Age-related hearing loss is nearly universal past 75, treatment penetration is low, and the product is almost entirely private-pay in most markets — which makes hearing the most reimbursement-insulated age curve available. Sonova is vertically integrated from chip to retail store, and the retail leg is what converts a hardware business into a recurring one. The two threats are real but slower than they look: over-the-counter hearing aids in the US compress the low end, and the emerging clinical link between untreated hearing loss and dementia progression could just as easily expand the market as commoditise it. Genuinely under-owned relative to how clean the demographic exposure is.

companies.name: Demant
companies.thesis_note: The other half of the hearing duopoly-plus, with the same demographic exposure and the same private-pay insulation. Slightly less vertically integrated on retail than Sonova, which makes it more dependent on independent audiologist channels — themselves a limb C shortage.

companies.name: Amplifon
companies.thesis_note: The pure retail and audiology-service layer of the hearing market, consolidating a fragmented store base across Europe and beyond. Owns the customer relationship rather than the technology, which is the better position when the hardware commoditises but the worse one if direct-to-consumer channels disintermediate the store.

companies.name: Cochlear
companies.thesis_note: Dominant in cochlear implants, with a large and almost entirely untapped adult and elderly severe-hearing-loss population — adult penetration is a small fraction of the eligible pool. Recurring sound-processor upgrade revenue on a growing installed base is a genuine annuity. Persistently among the most expensive medtech assets anywhere.
companies.froth_note: Quality and demographic exposure both excellent; valuation has been demanding for a decade and remains so.

companies.name: Straumann Holding
companies.thesis_note: Tooth loss is an age curve and implants are the premium treatment for it — almost entirely private-pay, which is the insulation this universe values. The catch is that private-pay means discretionary: implant volumes are visibly sensitive to consumer confidence, so this is the go-go band's wallet rather than the no-go band's medical necessity. A wealth-effect trade wearing a demographic costume.

companies.name: ResMed
companies.thesis_note: Sleep apnoea and COPD prevalence both rise with age, and the razor-and-blade mask resupply model produces genuinely recurring revenue. This is also the cleanest listed instrument for the GLP-1 morbidity question: the market repriced ResMed sharply on the theory that weight-loss drugs shrink the apnoea population, and subsequent evidence has been more nuanced than that. Whatever your view, watching this equity is watching the market price limb D's falsifier in real time.

companies.name: Dexcom
companies.thesis_note: Type 2 diabetes prevalence rises with age and CGM penetration in the non-insulin-using population is early. The GLP-1 relationship cuts both ways and has whipsawed the equity repeatedly — more diagnosed and engaged patients versus a healthier long-run population. Genuine uncertainty rather than a knowable answer.

companies.name: Boston Scientific
companies.thesis_note: Atrial fibrillation prevalence roughly doubles with each decade after 65, and Boston Scientific leads the pulsed-field ablation cycle treating it — a textbook limb D volume story. Also holds urology and continence franchises with the same age exposure. The execution has been outstanding and the multiple now reflects that fully.
companies.froth_note: Best-executing large-cap medtech; nothing about the demographics is undiscovered at this price.

companies.name: Medtronic
companies.thesis_note: Broad exposure to essentially every age-driven procedure category — cardiac rhythm, structural heart, spine, diabetes, neuromodulation. That breadth is the problem for a thesis holding: the demographic signal is diversified away and the equity trades on execution and portfolio management. Cheap, yielding, and unexciting.

companies.name: Paramount Bed Holdings
companies.thesis_note: Dominant in Japanese hospital and nursing-care beds — the physical infrastructure of the no-go band, in the country that reached it first. The Japan-template value here is informational as much as financial: this is what demand looks like on the other side of the demographic transition the US is entering.

companies.name: Eli Lilly
companies.thesis_note: Holds both sides of limb D's central uncertainty in one company. Donanemab addresses early Alzheimer's — the largest unmet cost in the no-go band and the condition that drives memory-care demand. Meanwhile the GLP-1 franchise is the single most plausible agent of morbidity compression, which is limb D's stated falsifier. Owning Lilly is a partial hedge against your own care-volume book, which is an unusual and useful property. Valuation prices the obesity franchise for near-perfection.
companies.froth_note: Among the most crowded large-cap positions in global equities. The thesis-hedge property is real; the entry price is not attractive on any demographic argument.

companies.name: Biogen
companies.thesis_note: Leqembi, partnered with Eisai, is a direct play on the largest cost pool in the no-go band. Uptake has been slowed by infusion capacity, PET and CSF diagnostic bottlenecks and neurologist availability — which is limb C constraining limb D in an unusually literal way. The legacy multiple sclerosis base is in structural decline underneath it.

companies.name: Regeneron Pharmaceuticals
companies.thesis_note: Wet age-related macular degeneration and diabetic macular oedema are pure age curves and Eylea has been the standard of care. Included for the demographic exposure, but this is a patent-cliff and biosimilar-erosion story first — the pipeline decides the equity, not the demography.

companies.name: Welltower
companies.thesis_note: The best-positioned owner of senior housing in the world and the clearest statement of limb H's cyclical case: construction starts collapsed in 2020-2023, the 80+ population arrives regardless of what got built, and occupancy plus rate growth compound against a fixed supply. Welltower's shift toward operating-partnership structures means it captures that operating upside rather than collecting a flat rent — which is the right structure in an up-cycle and the wrong one when labour costs bite. That is the tension: this is an operating business dressed as real estate, and its largest input cost is exactly the wage inflation limb C predicts. The demographic story here is completely discovered and the equity is priced as a premium compounder.
companies.froth_note: The single most consensus expression of the entire boomerification thesis. Structurally excellent, priced for the supply-demand gap to persist without labour cost catching up.

companies.name: Ventas
companies.thesis_note: The second large senior housing platform, with the same supply-trough tailwind and a somewhat cheaper entry than Welltower, offset by a more mixed portfolio and a less dominant operator roster. The relative-value trade within the sector rather than the sector's best asset.

companies.name: CareTrust REIT
companies.thesis_note: Net-lease landlord to skilled nursing operators, spun out of Ensign and retaining that operating heritage in its underwriting. The net-lease structure is deliberately the opposite bet to Welltower's: it forgoes operating upside in exchange for insulation from the labour cost problem, taking tenant credit risk instead. In a thesis where limb C threatens operator margins, being the landlord rather than the operator is a defensible choice.

companies.name: Omega Healthcare Investors
companies.thesis_note: High-yielding skilled nursing landlord — the income expression of the care-demand thesis, which also makes it a limb A holding for the same investor. The yield exists because tenant credit is the risk: SNF operators live on Medicaid rates, and a state budget squeeze arrives as a rent coverage problem here. Being paid to wait is exactly what weakness w1 asks for.

companies.name: National Health Investors
companies.thesis_note: Smaller diversified healthcare REIT recovering from tenant-restructuring problems, with a senior housing operating portfolio that gives some exposure to the occupancy recovery. Cheaper for reasons that are legible in the tenant roster.

companies.name: Sabra Health Care REIT
companies.thesis_note: Mixed skilled nursing, senior housing and behavioural health portfolio at a higher yield and lower quality than the majors. The behavioural health exposure is a genuinely different demand driver that does not belong to this thesis.

companies.name: Brookdale Senior Living
companies.thesis_note: The largest US senior living operator and the highest-operational-leverage way to own limb H: occupancy recovering from pandemic lows into a supply-starved market, with a fixed cost base that means every incremental point of occupancy drops disproportionately to the bottom line. It is also the most direct collision between limbs C and H in the universe — the business is a labour business, and wage inflation eats the occupancy gain. Levered, contested, and genuinely binary depending on which of those two forces moves faster.

companies.name: PulteGroup
companies.thesis_note: Owns Del Webb, the defining active-adult brand in the US and the housing product the go-go band actually buys. The demographic argument is that 55+ buyers are less mortgage-rate-sensitive than first-time buyers because they are trading equity from an existing home rather than borrowing from scratch — which is a real and testable advantage in a high-rate environment. The offset is that the go-go band is the band that stops growing after 2030, so this tailwind has a visible expiry.

companies.name: Taylor Morrison Home
companies.thesis_note: Meaningful active-adult and resort-lifestyle exposure aimed at the wealthier end of the go-go band. Smaller and cheaper than Pulte with the same demographic driver and less brand equity in the 55+ category specifically.

companies.name: Equity LifeStyle Properties
companies.thesis_note: Ground-lease communities concentrated in retirement destinations — the affordable housing answer for the median retiree, which is the segment the thesis says is chronically under-served. Rent growth has been remarkably consistent because residents own the home and cannot easily move it, which is exceptional pricing power. Concentrated in Florida, so insurance cost and climate risk are real and rising line items.

companies.name: Sun Communities
companies.thesis_note: Same manufactured-housing logic as ELS with additional RV and marina exposure — which is go-go band discretionary rather than housing necessity, and therefore fades on the same clock. Portfolio simplification is the current management story.

companies.name: The Home Depot
companies.thesis_note: The listed proxy for aging in place, which is the revealed preference of essentially the entire cohort. Grab bars, walk-in showers, ramps, stair rails, single-floor conversions and the ageing-homeowner repair cycle all run through here, and increasingly through the professional installer channel as the cohort stops doing it themselves — which is itself a limb C demand driver. The demographic contribution is real but diluted inside a very large housing-cycle business.

companies.name: Lowe's Companies
companies.thesis_note: The same aging-in-place modification demand with a heavier DIY customer mix — which is arguably the wrong skew for this thesis, since the defining feature of the slow-go band is that it stops doing the work itself and hires someone. Building out the professional channel to address exactly that.

companies.name: Installed Building Products
companies.thesis_note: Installation-services rollup whose scarce asset is crews, not products — a limb C business inside the housing vertical. Currently levered to new residential construction rather than to retrofit, which is the wrong end of the demographic story; the aging-in-place retrofit market is the option, not the base case.

companies.name: Finance of America Companies
companies.thesis_note: The dominant reverse mortgage originator, and structurally the most direct answer to the median retiree's actual problem: asset-rich in a house, cash-poor in retirement, and unwilling to move. The product's reputational history is genuinely bad and the industry has repeatedly failed to convert demographic logic into a durable business. High-risk, high-optionality, and a good instrument for tracking whether home equity extraction finally becomes mainstream.

companies.name: Leggett & Platt
companies.thesis_note: Adjustable bed bases are an aging-in-place product with a demographic curve behind them. Everything else about the company — leverage, restructuring, cyclical furniture and automotive components exposure — dominates. On the map as a category marker rather than a recommendation.

companies.name: Viking Holdings
companies.thesis_note: The single most precisely targeted business in this universe: Viking admits no passengers under 18 and markets exclusively to affluent older travellers. That focus produced exceptional pricing power and returns through the go-go band's peak. It is also the sharpest illustration of limb D's sequencing warning — the population Viking sells to peaks around 2030 and then declines, and the company's entire competitive advantage is its refusal to serve anyone else. A superb business trading against an expiring demographic clock.
companies.froth_note: Priced on the strength of a booking curve that reflects the go-go band at its peak. This is the definitional 'fade into strength' name.

companies.name: Royal Caribbean Cruises
companies.thesis_note: Broader demographic mix than Viking, with genuine multigenerational and family demand that partially insulates it from the go-go band's decline — the private-destination strategy is a real differentiator. Still, the core cruise customer skews old, and the equity has re-rated enormously on a booking cycle powered by the band that is about to shrink.
companies.froth_note: Cycle-peak earnings on cycle-peak multiples with the demographic support turning. Hard to own here on this thesis.

companies.name: Carnival Corporation
companies.thesis_note: The value end of cruising, serving the median retiree rather than the affluent one — which is a different and arguably more durable customer, since cruising is genuinely cheap holiday for someone on a fixed income. Deleveraging story dominates. Same expiring band, less premium exposure.

companies.name: Thor Industries
companies.thesis_note: RV buying is a go-go band behaviour with a hard biological limit — people stop driving large vehicles in their late seventies. Deeply cyclical, currently depressed, and the structural demographic support weakens exactly as any cyclical recovery would arrive. A cheap cyclical, not a thesis long.

companies.name: Brunswick Corporation
companies.thesis_note: Boating skews old and wealthy — a top-decile go-go purchase. The engine and parts business provides a recurring aftermarket base that cushions the cycle. Same expiring demographic band as RVs, with the same conclusion.

companies.name: Acushnet Holdings
companies.thesis_note: Golf participation is heavily weighted to older affluent men and the dedicated-golfer customer is remarkably price-insensitive. Post-pandemic participation gains have held better than expected, which is the bull case. The core customer band still contracts after 2030.

companies.name: Kimberly-Clark
companies.thesis_note: Adult incontinence is one of the most reliable demographic volume curves in consumer staples and one of the least discussed, for obvious reasons. Depend and Poise are category-defining brands. The problem for a thesis holding is dilution: adult care is a modest share of a company still dominated by tissue and baby care, where the baby category faces the opposite demographic force. Own it for the read-through, or wait for a structural separation.

companies.name: Essity
companies.thesis_note: TENA is the global leader in incontinence care, and Essity's mix is far more weighted to health and medical hygiene than Kimberly-Clark's — which makes it the cleaner listed expression of the same demographic curve. Sells heavily into institutional care settings, so it grows with the no-go population and with care facility census directly.

companies.name: Unicharm
companies.thesis_note: The single most instructive company in the entire universe. Unicharm's adult incontinence sales surpassed its baby nappy sales in Japan in 2011 — the most vivid available proof of what the demographic transition does to a consumer basket. Adult products are now roughly a third of Japanese net sales, up from an estimated quarter in 2018, in a category growing 6–10% a year at price points reported as high as 2.5x infant equivalents. Watching that mix is watching the US cohort's future arrive early. Asian emerging-market growth drives the equity today, which dilutes the demographic purity.

companies.name: McKesson
companies.thesis_note: Prescription volume per capita rises steeply with age, and distribution is a volume-and-mix business with almost no exposure to drug pricing itself — which is precisely the structural insulation limb E argues for. Oligopoly economics, minimal capital intensity, relentless buybacks. The demographic tailwind here is slow, boring and remarkably reliable.

companies.name: Cencora
companies.thesis_note: The same distribution oligopoly with a heavier specialty and oncology mix — and cancer incidence is itself an age curve, so the specialty skew arguably improves the demographic exposure rather than diluting it. Same volume-not-price insulation from limb E.

companies.name: Cardinal Health
companies.thesis_note: The third distributor, historically the weakest operator of the three, with a medical-products segment that has been a persistent drag and a turnaround that has been genuinely improving. Same structural demographic exposure at a lower quality of execution.

companies.name: CVS Health
companies.thesis_note: Owns pharmacy, a large Medicare Advantage insurer and senior primary care assets — every part of the cohort's healthcare interaction in one company. In practice the vertical integration has destroyed rather than created value, and the MA exposure delivered exactly the limb E outcome the thesis warns about. Cheap for reasons.

companies.name: Dollar General
companies.thesis_note: The median-retiree consumption trade, and a deliberately unglamorous one. Small-format stores in rural and small-town locations serve a fixed-income customer who cannot easily drive to a supercentre — a customer base the thesis says grows in number and gets poorer in real terms as limb E bites. Execution has been poor and the competitive position is contested, but the demographic and income logic is sound.

companies.name: Chewy
companies.thesis_note: An indirect and genuinely underrated angle: empty-nest and newly-retired households are heavy pet spenders, and the autoship subscription model plus home delivery suits an older customer who values not carrying heavy bags. Pet pharmacy adds a recurring healthcare-like layer. Thin demographic evidence relative to the story, so treated as speculative.

companies.name: Service Corporation International
companies.thesis_note: The largest death-care operator in North America, and the most mathematically certain demand curve in the universe — deaths in the cohort are the one variable that cannot be deferred, substituted or reformed away. Two features make it more than a morbid annuity. Preneed sales create a large deferred revenue backlog that converts on a predictable lag, effectively pre-funding future volume at today's prices. And cemetery property is an appreciating, irreplaceable asset in supply-constrained metros. The genuine structural threat is mix, not volume: cremation rates keep rising and cremation revenue per case is far lower than burial, so the company has to grow volume and premium service attach faster than mix erodes. That race is the whole investment case.

companies.name: Carriage Services
companies.thesis_note: The smaller consolidator in the same death-care demographics, running a decentralised model that gives local funeral home managers real autonomy — which matters in a business built on community relationships. More levered than SCI and more exposed to the same cremation mix shift, with more room to compound through acquisition.

companies.name: Matthews International
companies.thesis_note: Supplies caskets, memorial products and cremation equipment — which is an elegant partial hedge against the mix shift that threatens SCI, since Matthews sells into both burial and cremation. The complication is that a large part of the company is an unrelated industrial technology business, and the capital structure has been the dominant issue rather than the demographics.
